kpis.name: Smart energy revenue share
kpis.definition: Measures the share of total revenue from grid equipment and automation, energy efficiency products, demand response, battery storage and inverters, as disclosed in segment or product line reporting. Companies whose revenue comes only from EV manufacturing or fossil fuel production score at the bottom.

levels.0: Disclosed segments show under 5% of revenue from smart energy products or services, or the business is a pure EV maker or pure fossil fuel producer.
levels.1: Smart energy segments or product lines make up 5% to under 15% of revenue, for example a disclosed grid or storage line inside a broader industrial group.
levels.2: Smart energy segments make up 15% to under 30% of revenue, according to segment or product line disclosure.
levels.3: Smart energy segments make up 30% to under 50% of revenue, according to segment disclosure.
levels.4: Smart energy segments make up 50% or more of revenue, and segment tables back this up.

rubric.unknown: Return unknown if the filing has no segment, product line or revenue breakdown that allows the smart energy share to be estimated, or if no filing text is available for the company.

extraction.target: Revenue from grid equipment and automation, energy efficiency, demand response, battery storage and inverter products and services, divided by total company revenue, for the latest fiscal year.

kpis.name: Committed capital and backlog in smart energy
kpis.definition: Assesses whether the company has committed capital, capacity expansion or order backlog to smart energy products, based on cited filing passages. Credit goes only to named projects, plants, acquisitions or backlog figures.

levels.0: No passage names investment, capacity, acquisitions or orders related to grid, efficiency, demand response, storage or inverter products.
levels.1: Smart energy appears only as a stated strategic priority or target, with no amount, named project or backlog figure.
levels.2: At least one named smart energy project, plant expansion or acquisition is disclosed, without a monetary amount, or with an amount under 5% of annual revenue.
levels.3: Disclosed smart energy capex, acquisitions or order backlog with a stated monetary amount of 5% to 20% of annual revenue.
levels.4: Disclosed smart energy capex programmes, acquisitions or backlog with a stated monetary amount above 20% of annual revenue, or a multi-year plan whose committed amounts are tied to smart energy segments.

rubric.unknown: Return unknown if no filing text is available, or if the retrieved passages discuss capital allocation without saying which products or segments it serves.

kpis.name: Grid equipment and automation offering
kpis.definition: Assesses how central grid equipment, substation and distribution automation, grid software and smart metering are to the company's products, based on cited filing passages. Second-order component suppliers can earn the middle levels.

levels.0: No named grid equipment, automation, grid software or metering product or customer.
levels.1: Supplies components or materials such as cables, semiconductors or enclosures, and the filing names grid or utility customers as one end market among several, with no figures.
levels.2: Names at least one grid equipment, automation or metering product line, or names utilities as a disclosed end market with a revenue share figure.
levels.3: Reports a grid or electrification segment, or named grid automation products, with a disclosed revenue or order figure.

kpis.name: Energy efficiency and demand response offering
kpis.definition: Assesses how central energy efficiency and demand response products and services are to the company, based on cited filing passages. Examples include building and industrial energy management systems, efficient drives and motors, and demand response platforms.

levels.0: No named energy efficiency or demand response product, service or programme.
levels.1: Supplies components used in efficiency products, or mentions efficiency as a product feature, with no named product line or figures.
levels.2: Names at least one efficiency or demand response product line or programme, such as energy management software, variable speed drives or a utility demand response contract, without revenue figures.
levels.3: Names efficiency or demand response product lines and gives a revenue, order, contracted capacity or installed base figure for them.
levels.4: Efficiency or demand response is a reported segment or more than half of revenue, backed by segment figures.

rubric.unknown: Return unknown if no filing text is available, or if the efficiency claims cannot be linked to a named product or service.

kpis.name: Storage and inverter offering
kpis.definition: Assesses how central battery storage systems, inverters and power conversion for renewables and grids are to the company, based on cited filing passages. Second-order cell, component and materials suppliers can earn the middle levels.

levels.1: Supplies materials or components such as semiconductors or cells, and names storage or solar inverters as one end market among several, with no figures.

framework.rationale: The disclosed smart energy revenue share carries the most weight (30%) because it is the most direct and checkable measure of exposure, and committed capital and backlog (20%) captures the five year horizon. The three segment KPIs (50% together) let broad, second-order suppliers earn middle levels. No KPI is a gate, because broad style should not exclude small suppliers, and the exclusions are already enforced by level 0 in the revenue share rubric. None of the registered quant functions measures smart energy exposure directly, so all KPIs use filing text; Swiss names such as ABB and German names will be scored unknown rather than filled with market factors, and the PM should review them manually.

Our Company
We are a global energy technology company originally founded in March 2006. We deliver smart, easy-to-use solutions that manage solar generation, storage and communication on one platform. Our intelligent microinverters work with virtually every solar panel made, and when paired with our smart technology, result in one of the industry’s best-performing clean energy systems.
For the first time in the evolution of our centuries-old grid, people can get paid for the clean energy they produce and share with their communities, helping to build a new energy future that harnesses the sun. This clean, free, abundant source of energy can power our lives and ultimately help greatly reduce our dependence on fossil fuels. As of December 31, 2025, we have shipped approximately 86.4 million microinverters, and more than 5.1 million Enphase residential and commercial systems have been deployed in over 160 countries.
We design, develop, manufacture and sell home energy solutions that manage energy generation, energy storage, and control and communications on one intelligent platform. We have revolutionized the solar industry by bringing a systems approach to solar technology and by pioneering a semiconductor-based microinverter that converts energy at the individual solar module level and, combined with our proprietary networking and software technologies, provides advanced energy monitoring and control. This is vastly different than a string inverter system using string modules, whether with or without an optimizer, which only converts the energy of the entire array of solar modules from a single high voltage electrical unit and lacks intelligence about the energy producing capacity of the solar array.
The Enphase® Energy System brings a high technology, networked approach to solar generation plus energy storage, by leveraging our design expertise across power electronics, semiconductors and cloud-based software technologies. Our integrated approach to energy solutions maximizes a home’s energy potential while providing advanced monitoring and remote maintenance capabilities. The Enphase Energy System uses a single technology platform for seamless management of the whole solution, of IQ® Microinverters, IQ® Batteries, IQ® Load Controllers, and IQ® EV Charger, allowing rapid commissioning with the Enphase® Installer App, consumption monitoring with our IQ® Combiner™ device with our Enphase IQ® Gateway™ device, and our Enphase® App, a cloud-based energy management platform. System owners can use the Enphase App to monitor their home’s solar generation, energy storage and consumption from any web-enabled device. Unlike some of our competitors, who utilize a traditional inverter, or offer separate components of solutions, we have built-in system redundancy in both photovoltaic (“PV”) generation and energy storage, eliminating the risk that comes with a single point of failure. Further, the nature of our cloud-based, monitored system allows for remote firmware and software updates, enabling cost-effective remote maintenance and ongoing utility compliance.

One Big Beautiful Bill Act. In July 2025, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (the “OBBBA”) was enacted, introducing material changes to certain federal clean energy tax credit programs that are significant to our business and may impact our financial condition, results of operations and future prospects.
The OBBBA scales back the Investment Tax Credit (the “ITC”) available under Section 25D of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), for residential solar and storage systems purchased through cash or loans. Under the new law, the Section 25D credit expired on December 31, 2025. In addition, the OBBBA imposes new timing requirements for eligibility under Section 48E of the Code, which governs ITCs for leased solar and storage systems. Specifically, solar-only projects that do not commence construction within 12 months of the OBBBA’s enactment must be placed in service by December 31, 2027 in order to remain eligible for the credit. Energy storage projects are not subject to this placed-in-service deadline; however, the ITC for storage systems will begin to phase down in 2034 — decreasing to 75% in 2034, 50% in 2035 and phasing out entirely by 2036.
The OBBBA also amends the domestic content bonus credit rules for Section 48E projects. Projects commencing construction after June 16, 2025 must meet a 45% domestic cost threshold, up from 40%.
Additionally, the OBBBA introduces new compliance requirements under the Foreign Entity of Concern (“FEOC”) provisions for both Section 48E and the Advanced Manufacturing Production Tax Credit (“AMPTC”) under Section 45X of the Code. These provisions establish an escalating threshold of non-FEOC content that must be met by solar and storage projects beginning construction in 2026 and by manufactured components produced beginning in 2026.
On July 7, 2025, the President issued an Executive Order directing the Secretary of the Treasury to issue updated guidance within 45 days on the “beginning of construction” requirements applicable to Section 48E projects. In August 2025, Treasury and the IRS issued revised “beginning of construction” guidance for clean energy tax credits that only applies to projects above 1MW. The Executive Order also requires the Secretary to implement the FEOC restrictions set forth in the OBBBA. Additional guidance around FEOC is still forthcoming and is expected to be finalized in 2026, which could make existing requirements more stringent.
